title: Dietary and Microbial Determinants of Intestinal Sulfur Gas and Malodor: Mechanisms, Phenotypes, and Nutritional Mitigation.
abstract: Intestinal gas and malodor are common nutrition-related concerns that may influence dietary adherence, gastrointestinal symptoms, and quality of life. Although gas volume and odor are often treated as a single outcome, they arise from partly distinct processes. Bulk intestinal gas is generated principally through swallowed air, acid-bicarbonate reactions, and microbial fermentation, whereas malodor is determined mainly by trace volatile sulfur compounds, including hydrogen sulfide, methanethiol, and dimethyl sulfide. Their production depends on dietary sulfur amino acids, sulfate, taurine, host-derived substrates, microbial cross-feeding, intestinal transit, luminal chemistry, and gas-liquid partitioning. This review integrates evidence concerning dietary determinants of intestinal gas, gut microbial sulfur metabolism, nutritional and microbiome-directed interventions, and downstream odor-control strategies. The concept of conditional sound-odor discordance is retained as a secondary framework illustrating that gas volume, acoustic intensity, and odor burden should not be considered interchangeable endpoints. Human dietary trials indicate that low-FODMAP diets and substrate-specific enzymes may reduce fermentation-related symptoms or total gas production, but they do not necessarily suppress sulfur-derived odorants. Probiotic evidence remains strain-specific and largely indirect, whereas sulfide-binding compounds and external adsorptive devices target odor-active molecules more directly. Future nutritional studies should combine controlled dietary exposure with measurements of gas volume, volatile sulfur compounds, microbial functional pathways, intestinal transit, and perceived odor.

title: Subpopulation networks: a scaling principle for engineering living systems.
authors: Delvigne Frank; Roeloffs Fabian; Josselin Laurie; Pressé Steve; Olsson Lisbeth et al.
abstract: Cell populations underpin applications ranging from bioproduction and biotherapeutics to microbiome engineering and biocomputing. However, treating them as bulk quantities rather than as structured systems limits our understanding of population-level stability, productivity, and robustness. Cellular populations self-organize into coexisting subpopulations (SPs) representing phenotypically distinct states that emerge from the interplay of biological noise and selective pressures. We propose that networks of interacting SPs constitute a fundamental organizational layer for engineering stable cell population dynamics. Surveying published single-cell studies across bacterial, yeast, and mammalian systems, we show that populations consistently self-organize into a limited number of SPs. This dimensional reduction can be captured experimentally by clustering single-cell data and gives rise to scaling laws that link population structure to collective performance.

title: Myeloid cell reprogramming drives enhanced defense against Streptococcus pneumoniae lung infection following exposure to commensal Prevotella.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
authors: Stoner Sara N; Larson Eric D; Fulte Sam; Shaw Steven C; Fish Erin R et al.
abstract: Clinical data link the prevalent respiratory tract anaerobe Prevotella with reduced pneumonia mortality, but the mechanisms directing Prevotella regulation of lung immune homeostasis are unclear. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing was employed to define the transcriptional immune signatures underlying improved clearance of Streptococcus pneumoniae following lung exposure to Prevotella melaninogenica. Overall, we observed a substantial shift in myeloid cell transcriptional programming from interferon-dominant to a more antibacterial profile in S. pneumoniae-infected mice after pre-exposure to P. melaninogenica, correlating with increased macrophage and neutrophil phagocytosis of S. pneumoniae and improved pathogen clearance. In neutrophils, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling through TNFR2 was essential for increased antimicrobial function. Moreover, improved defense required CCR2-dependent monocyte-derived macrophages, with selective enrichment of more a mature Cxcl3+ population which was distinct from the hallmark S. pneumoniae-associated C1qa+ population enriched in the absence of effective clearance. Together, these findings inform the myeloid cell transcriptional changes associated with natural infection resistance mediated by pulmonary microbial exposures.

title: Differential effects of prenatal depression and anxiety on infant sleep: dual-pathway mechanisms involving the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the gut-brain axis.
authors: Liu Can; Lin Yuan; Li Ye; Liu Ting; Yang Sukang et al.
abstract:
STUDY OBJECTIVES: Prenatal psychological distress is associated with adverse offspring outcomes, including infant sleep disturbances (ISD) and altered gut microbiota, yet the mediating roles of the neonatal gut microbiome and tryptophan metabolism remain underexplored.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective birth cohort study enrolled 2288 mother-infant pairs, using questionnaires to assess prenatal anxiety/depression and infant sleep patterns up to 12 months. A 112-pair sub-cohort underwent multi-omics analyses: meconium microbiota profiling via 16S rRNA sequencing and cord blood tryptophan metabolite quantification via liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, mediation analyses, and XGBoost modeling were applied.
RESULTS: Prenatal depression alone was a significant risk factor for ISD (fully adjusted OR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.04-2.25), with a stronger effect in female infants (OR = 2.11, p = .022). Cord blood cortisol partially mediated this link (Average Causal Mediation Effect = -7.47, 95% CI: [-14.82, -0.12], p = .048). Prenatal anxiety correlated with reduced meconium microbial alpha-diversity, lower Bifidobacterium abundance, and decreased 3-HAA/serotonin levels, which were associated with sleep disturbance; serial mediation confirmed the gut microbiota-tryptophan metabolism pathway. The XGBoost predictive model achieved an AUC of 0.727, with microbial diversity, Streptococcus abundance, dopamine, and 3-HAA as top contributors.
CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies distinct mediating pathways for depression and anxiety, providing targets for personalized infant sleep health interventions. Statement of Significance This study reveals that prenatal depression and anxiety impair infant sleep through distinct biological pathways. Depression was associated with elevated fetal cortisol (HPA axis), while anxiety may influence the neonatal gut microbiome and its production of sleep-regulating tryptophan metabolites. These findings contribute to a novel dual-pathway model that helps clarify previously unresolved mechanistic questions. By integrating these biomarkers into a machine learning model, we offer a translational tool for early risk prediction. The work bridges a critical gap between epidemiological observation and biological mechanism, paving the way for personalized interventions-targeting stress hormones for depression or gut health for anxiety-to improve infant neurodevelopmental outcomes.

title: Nanoformulated Curcumin Ameliorates Ulcerative Colitis via Gut Microbiota Modulation and Barrier Function Restoration.
journal: The American journal of Chinese medicine
authors: Xie Yin-Zhuo; Sun Chen-Xi; Fu Tian-Tian; Jin Zheng; Nalinratana Nonthaneth et al.
abstract: The gut microbiota is increasingly recognized as a key mediator of the anticolitis effects of curcumin (CUR). However, the clinical translation of this promising activity is severely hampered by CUR's low solubility and poor bioavailability. Although nanoencapsulation represents a promising strategy to address these limitations, the preventive effect of nanocurcumin (nano-CUR) against colitis remains largely unexplored. The present study aimed to elucidate the preventive effects of nano-CUR on intestinal barrier function, gut microbiota composition, and metabolic profiles in a murine model of dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis. The results demonstrated that pre-supplementation of nano-CUR significantly ameliorated disease severity, attenuated intestinal barrier disruption, and suppressed colonic inflammation in mice with DSS-induced colitis. Mechanistically, integrated 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics demonstrated that nano-CUR-restored microbial homeostasis and enhanced the production of short-chain fatty acids, linking microbial shifts to anti-inflammatory outcomes. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) further validated the causal role of the nano-CUR-remodeled microbiota in conferring protection. Collectively, these findings decipher the mechanism by which nano-CUR interacts with the gut microbiota, confirming that dietary nano-CUR consumption protects against ulcerative colitis by modulating the gut microbiome and its metabolic output.
